content.title: Technical correctness and usefulness of the proposed add-ons need further justification.
content.review:
The paper addresses zero-shot neural architecture search (NAS), where the zero-shot NAS approach was first proposed in a closely related arXiv paper, cited as [4] and also under review for ICLR 2021. The main effort here is to extend the Jacobian score (JS) function in [4] to several variants and compare their NAS performance. While the improvements seem to be marginal, the presentation of the paper can be improved to better characterize the technical contributions of the proposed modifications over [4].

Main concerns about the technical correctness and contributions of the proposed techniques are listed below.
1. In JSC, page 3, it is claimed that the time complexity for calculating JSC is O(B \log B) and should be significantly faster than O(B^3) as in the original JS. However, such speed-up has not been observed in the experimental results (Figure 3).
2. In SNS, page 3, the noisy data are formed by adding noise in proportion to the variance rather than the standard deviation.  Could the authors explain the reasoning?
3. It is hard to comprehend the explanations and the indexing notations about the parameters-related score functions (PJS, page 3). Even more confusing is that the authors did not explicitly explain how the various parameters tensors are computed under the setting of zero-shot NAS, i.e., without any network training.
4. The two weighing schemes (WPJS and WPJSI) are opposite to each other but give similar performance. What are the reasonable explanations here?
5. The experimental results are not convincing.  First, the claimed time efficiency over JS has not been observed. Second, the validity of the experimental results from those parameters-related score functions need to be justified. Third, the usefulness of the monotonicity criterion is not evident from Figure 4 and the minor improvements in NAS. 
6. More detailed quantitative results and comparisons about the achieved accuracies from the yielded NAS architectures with respect to those by [4] and SOTA NAS techniques should be provided.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: first reply
content.comment:
1. there is an improvement in speed, for every variation that has a C at the end, with respect to the one without a C, but the experimental evidence suggests it is not a game changer, you are right, I will mention it clearly in the discussion.
2. many formalizations of noise would have been able to capture the intuition that distorsion of the input could be insightful, but it is true that the standard deviation would have been probably the best choice.
3. Interesting, I'll find a way to be more clear in the next upload. I think I tried to use a more physics oriented indexing, but I see that it can be confusing. For the second part of the comment, we used NAS-Bench-201, where they provide the initialized network and their final performance, among others, for 15K nets, on the three dataset that we used, CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and ImageNet16. The gradients can then be calculated and used before applying the update rule on the parameters (training). I was trying to explain this point in section 3.1, but probably I could be more clear.
4. I mention at the beginning of page 7 that an improvement over PJS was observed as well when a change in the normalization was performed to resemble WPJS and WPJSI. However I can't see what could be a reasonable explanation for that.
5. it is true that improvements seem small, however we thought that figure 3 left shows a clear improvement, both in the best architecture found and the variance in the decision. Another observation that we found remarkable is this extract from the paper "It is remarkable as well that both WPJS and WPJSI placed the best architecture in the 1000 architectures sample, within the top 1.6 percentile in the score, for the three datasets, while the original JS score placed the best architecture within the 30.8 percentile.". We designed the monotonicity score because when you look at the data closely, at different scales, it is easy to convince yourself that JS is very flat, while the rest are less, but in one snapshot like in figure 2, where the y limits are chosen to match those in the left figure, it becomes really hard to see.
6. to reply to this comment, we performed the scores on alexnet, vgg16, vgg19, resnet50, resnet152, densenet201, efficientnet-b0 and efficientnet-b1 for ImageNet 224x224, and the only ones capable to order them almost perfectly were WPJS and WPJSI. We have performed as well the metrics for language models in the dataset NAS-Bench-NLP, where the metrics performed in the input space are not even applicable, given that the input is non differentiable. We propose slight modifications to be able to still run them, but scores in the parameter space perform better. We would add both figures in the next upload.

content.title: Review of "Improving Zero-Shot Neural Architecture Search with Parameters Scoring"
content.review:
The authors consider the case of zero-shot neural architecture search. In this task, a function of the network is computed before training, and the objective is to determine whether this score is a consistent predictor of good performance after training.

The strengths of the paper are:
- The field of application is interesting, and there are very few other papers on that topic (to the best of my knowledge).
- The paper is easy to follow.
- Some of the scores introduced by the authors achieve good performance with the chosen metric, and a detailed comparison is performed.

The negative aspects:
- Each score proposed is justified, but it feels as if there is no underlying unifying theory for the work. It's definitely interesting to see if different heuristics result in good downstream performance, but I feel a stronger paper would try to get a more important theoretical justification rather than a list of motivated scores, or at least an intuition.
- Results on the small architectures in the NAS-benchmark set are nice, but the paper would benefit from a comparison with larger, more realistic architectures. I would insist on the fact that this point is not however a deal-breaker for me.

(very) Minor point:
- The format for references seems wrong. I'm not sure about that aspect (so it did not weigh in my evaluation of the paper) ("(1)" versus "(name)"). Please disregard if wrong, or correct if true.

My present recommendation is a borderline reject. I like the paper, but don't feel it is currently strong enough to be accepted. I'm open to changing my opinion but will wait for the author's response, and the discussion with other reviewers before considering doing so. To address my points, I would encourage the authors to discuss in more detail what is to be gained theoretically from the empirical results they found. I understand this point is open-ended and might be somewhat difficult to address.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: first reply
content.comment:
1. I have been trying to mathematize the intuition I have of why JS works and why it should work better in parameter space, but I couldn't come up with something solid yet. I will give a better justification in the rebuttal, describing the intuition behind the good performance: perpendicular gradients might be the eraly signature of the attempt of the network to build disentangled representations, which will ease decision making after training. It is reasonable to assume that disentangled representations are more effective if they happen at every intermediate layer than if they happen only at the input: this is the intuition that led me to explore parameter space.
2. to reply to this comment, we performed the scores on alexnet, vgg16, vgg19, resnet50, resnet152, densenet201, efficientnet-b0 and efficientnet-b1 for ImageNet 224x224, and the only ones capable to order them almost perfectly were WPJS and WPJSI. We have performed as well the metrics for language models in the dataset NAS-Bench-NLP, where the metrics performed in the input space are not even applicable, given that the input is non differentiable. We propose slight modifications to be able to still run them, but scores in the parameter space perform better. We would add both figures in the next upload.
3. theoretically we can say that more is to be found about final performance in the early movements in parameter space rather than in input space. Perpendicular gradients might signal that the operations defined by the network are extremely reactive to that type of data. We could even venture that the network is trying to build disentangled representations, and the perpendicular gradients are an early signal. We will adress the theoretical justification in future work, as soon as we manage to find the good framework.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
Summary
   This paper builds on top of a zero-shot NAS paper [1]. In [1] they developed a metric based on the correlation matrix of the Jacobian wrt every datapoint for a batch. This paper conceived few other scores the predominant one being Jacobian Cosine (JC), Parameter based Jacobian Score (PJS), Weighted Parameter Jacobian Score (WPJS) and Weighted Parameters Jacobian Score Inverse (WPJSI).
JC: Rather than having to compute the computationally expensive correlation matrix, they recommended using cosine similarity for all pairs of Jacobians.
PJS: computes the Jacobian in Parameter space $\frac{\partial f} {\partial W}$ instead of wrt the input datapoint $\frac{\partial f} {\partial x_{i}}$
WPJS: While computing PJS, higher weights are assigned to the last few layers
WPJSI: While computing PJS, higher weights are assigned to the first few layers

Questions:

1. Are the images in a batch formed by repeatedly augmenting an image using cut-out ? The first-few ones which rely on Jacobian wrt datapoint at least require that? If so, then can you empirically show that the quality of ranking does not depend on the image being used
2. For Jacobians wrt parameters, can you empirically show that the ranking is robust to various initializations?
3.  Could you also provide the Kendall Tau scores for correlation between the rankings using each metric vs that using the validation accuracy in a table? Also the monotonicity for the ranking of architecture above the median score seem to have dropped drastically. Are these metrics effective enough to rank networks whose performance is close to each other?

While the paper is a step in the right direction to reduce the computational budget, the effectiveness of these metrics is still questionable.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

1. in our experiments batches are of 256 16x16 images, but they are all different, so not the same image with its cut-outs. 2. ideally it would be a very interesting study to perform, but each one of the 15K architectures was run only once in the original NAS-Bench-201 work, which corresponds to one initialization and one final accuracy to predict. I would expect it to behave as the monotonicity then. I take figure 4 and 5 to be the reasons why in figure 3 left, the scores in parameter space find better performing architectures: given that their monotonicity stays stronger above the median score, those scores manage to find better top architectures. content.title: Improving Zero-Shot Neural Architecture Search with Parameters Scoring
content.review:
Summary:

 
The paper provides an interesting monotonicity metric to evaluate the adequate relative scoring of the architectures. Their exploration shows that the use of noise improves the score, and they observed a clear improvement when the evaluation
is done in the parameter space. The authors performed their experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet datasets. 

##########################################################################

Reasons for score: 

Overall, my score is more or less on the order but tend to see this work as a valuable contribution despite that I find some limitations in the paper. My major concern is about the clarity of the paper and some missing ablations.  Hopefully, the authors can address my concern in the rebuttal period. 
 

 
##########################################################################Pros: 

 
1. The paper takes one of the most important issues of neural architecture search: zero-shot NAS measuring the ability of the performance of a network in a task before the network is trained. For me, I find this problem of high importance and may encourage applying NAS to more problems/ applications. 

 
2. The paper explores twelve scoring metrics including the previously proposed JS score showing a reasonable depth in the possible scoring mechanisms to compare with.
 
3. This paper provides comprehensive experiments on these twelve metrics on three datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet). 
 They showed both the connection with accuracy and monotonicity of each score with respect to the accuracy.

 
##########################################################################

Cons: 

1. the explored metrics seem to need more discussion and more motivation. Some of them are reasonable but for others, more explanation is required why they are included. More discussion of why they perform well or bad is needed. 

2. I still suggest the authors conduct the following experiments studies to enhance the quality of the paper: 

(1) how does the metrics that use noise perform based on the scale of the noise $k=10^-6,10^-7,10^-8, 10^-5. 10^-4$

 
(2) can this score be used to improve AutoML zero? if so, would be interesting to do an experiment to study  if this may accelerating the learning process. 

AutoML-Zero: Evolving Machine Learning Algorithms From Scratch
https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03384, ICML, 2020 

 
3. How scalable is this approach to apply for full imageNet scale and perhaps multimodal tasks? What could go wrong?  

 
4. "An ideal slope is not necessarily 1 or -1, but at least should remain constant or high enough for different ranges of the
score, to ease its usability."
please elaborate more experimentally on the tradeoff and what it means.   


minor
--------------
there are big spaces between figures (e.g., Fig 3 and 4) and the remaining space can be used to enrich the paper (more discussions & insights).
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.comment:
1. that is true, we will address it in the next upload by appropriately motivating in the methodology and discussing in the discussion section.
2. 
  (1) the intention of using SNS, LNS and MNJS was that, but it is true that it needs a more detailed discussion, and it will be provided in the next upload.
  (2) very interesting article, I will read it and I will try to have something ready on the next upload.
3. following your comment we run our metrics on the state of the art architectures on ImageNet 224x224, and we found that WPJS and WPJSI are the ones that predict the best future accuracy, while the original JS saturates and is not informative. We performed as well the score on the language NAS-Bench-NLP, where the original JS is not applicable right away, since the input are the integers that represent the words, so it is not differentiable. We propose a small modification to be able to run the scores in the input space, but we still see a better performance in the parameter space.
4. you are right, that statement is unclear, I will rephrase it into  'a desirable property for a score is that a consistent slope should be maintained throughout its range, without drastic change for different percentiles'
